name: KP1 (Klotho-derived peptide 1)

track.title: Lab & animal
track.line: Mouse, rat and cell studies since 2022, mostly 1 group

track.title: Research use only
track.line: Not FDA approved; research labels not for humans

what.text: KP1 is a chain of 30 amino acids cut from the human klotho protein, from position 57 to 86. A kidney research group at Southern Medical University in Guangzhou, China, found it in 2022 by screening many klotho fragments. Klotho itself is a large protein, which the authors say is hard to use as a medicine.

src.label: Yuan et al., Nature Communications, 2022 (full text, PMC)

what.text: How it acts, according to animal and cell studies:

items.text: In kidney cells, KP1 bound to the TGF-β type 2 receptor and blocked TGF-β, a signal that drives scarring (fibrosis).
In mice, KP1 injected into a vein gathered mainly in injured kidneys and restored the kidneys’ own klotho.
In diseased mouse kidneys, it lowered markers of cell ageing (senescence), through a microRNA that blocks klotho.
In 2026, the same group reported that it binds a mitochondrial protein, ATAD3A, in kidney cells.

what.text: None of these effects has been tested in people.

research.text: Human evidence: none. No published human studies found as of November 1, 2026. All published KP1 studies are in mice, rats or cells, and almost all come from one research group in Guangzhou.
No published human studies found as of November 1, 2026. PubMed lists five KP1 papers, all in animals or cells, and ClinicalTrials.gov lists no trial.

research.title: Kidney scarring in mice

facts.v: Yuan Q, et al. Nat Commun 2022;13(1):438
controlled animal study, KP1 against vehicle, plus cell experiments
mouse models of kidney scarring: blocked ureter, and reduced blood flow to one kidney
KP1 1 mg/kg into a vein once a day, for 6 days in the blocked-ureter model
kidney function (creatinine, urea), scarring, TGF-β signalling, klotho levels

research.found: KP1 preserved kidney function, reduced scarring and restored kidney klotho in mice. The authors declared no competing interests.

src.label: Yuan et al., Nature Communications, 2022 (full text, PMC)

items.text: in mouse models of acute kidney injury from cisplatin or from cut-off blood flow, KP1 improved kidney function and reduced tubule cell death.
in mice made to express a SARS-CoV-2 protein, and in cells, KP1 reduced kidney tubule injury.
in klotho-deficient mice and in mice with chemical or bile-duct liver injury, KP1 reduced liver scarring.

src.label: Tan et al., Int J Biol Sci, 2026

items.text: in rats with cut penile nerves, a klotho-derived peptide reduced penile scarring and preserved erections. The abstract calls it “KP” and does not say whether it is KP1.

src.label: Xi et al., Eur J Pharmacol, 2026

research.text: These are animal and cell results from mostly one research group. They have not been tested in people.

us.text: Not FDA-approved for any use. No KP1 product appears in FDA’s drug approval database. Products labelled “research use only” are not for human use. As of November 1, 2026.

items.text: none. A search of Drugs@FDA for klotho found no match, and no KP1 trial is registered.

FDA says products marketed “for research use only” or otherwise not for human consumption “have not been evaluated for safety and should never be used by humans.” Such products may not be sold for human use: FDA says it acts against firms selling unapproved products.

after.title: Sport
after.text: KP1 is not named on the WADA Prohibited List for 2026 or 2027. WADA’s class S0 bans at all times any pharmacological substance not covered elsewhere on the List and with no current approval by any government health regulator for human use. For 2027, WADA adds “peptides” to the examples in S0. The lists do not say whether KP1 falls under S0.
Australia: KP1 is not named in the Poisons Standard that took effect on October 1, 2026. The TGA’s product register was not checked.

side.text: There are no human safety data. No one has published a study giving KP1 to people, and no formal animal toxicity studies were found.

items.text: the published papers test kidney, liver and nerve injury models over days to weeks. None was a standard toxicity study.

src.label: Tan et al., Int J Biol Sci, 2026

items.text: Health Canada warns that unauthorized injectable peptides may hold too much, too little or none of the ingredient, or contaminants. It says a “research use only” label does not make them legal.

unconfirmed: UK (MHRA) status and Australia’s TGA register were not checked against the regulator’s own record.
The 2026 rat study of erectile function calls its peptide “KP”; whether it is KP1 was not confirmed from the full text.
surprises: KP1 is promoted as a klotho-based anti-ageing peptide, but every published study is in mice, rats or cells, and almost all come from one lab group.
The published work is about kidney and liver scarring in injury models, not about ageing or lifespan.
